body_text: WOBURN, MA — Bridgeline Digital, Inc. (NASDAQ: BLIN), a leader in AI-powered product discovery and eCommerce solutions, announced today that a leading Ohio-based distributor serving the plumbing, HVAC, and electrical industries has successfully launched HawkSearch 90 days after project kickoff. The rapid deployment highlights Bridgeline’s ability to deliver fast time-to-value for complex B2B distributors modernizing digital commerce. The distributor operates 14 locations across Ohio and selected HawkSearch following a competitive evaluation. HawkSearch was chosen for its advanced category page functionality, out-of-the-box personalization, and ability to support B2B buying requirements such as customer-specific pricing, product restrictions, merchandising, and complex product data. “For distributors investing in digital commerce, speed-to-value matters just as much as functionality,” said Ari Kahn, President and CEO of Bridgeline. “This customer successfully moved from project kickoff to production launch in 90 days, demonstrating how quickly organizations can begin realizing value from HawkSearch. Rapid deployments like this help distributors improve the buying experience faster while creating a strong foundation for future expansion into advanced AI-powered capabilities.” Built for Complex B2B Product Discovery The deployment connects HawkSearch with the customer’s Unilog PIM and JD Edwards ERP systems, supporting a digital commerce experience built around complex catalog data, customer-specific pricing, product access rules, personalization, merchandising, analytics, and reporting. The customer selected HawkSearch to improve search relevance and conversion across its plumbing, HVAC, and electrical product catalog. Key capabilities include enhanced SKU and part-number search, machine learning-powered relevance, autocomplete, instant results, personalized recommendations, Unit of Measure normalization, and merchandising controls designed to reduce search friction and improve buyer engagement. Following the successful launch, the customer is evaluating additional HawkSearch capabilities including Smart Search, Smart Response, Recommendations, and advanced reporting, creating a potential path for broader AI-powered commerce adoption. Its HawkSearch platform delivers advanced search, personalization, and merchandising capabilities for B2B and B2C enterprises across high-growth industries. title: Pipedrive vs HubSpot vs Custom CRM: Real Costs, Features, and What Actually Fits in 2026
summary: Compare Pipedrive vs HubSpot vs custom CRM for 2026. Get clear on pricing, features, integrations, and long-term CRM costs for your business.
body_text: TL;DR: Pipedrive is more affordable and focused on sales simplicity, HubSpot delivers broader features but can become costly and complex, and a custom CRM like Miniloop offers workflow flexibility and significant savings for businesses with high CRM spend in 2026. Pipedrive vs HubSpot vs Custom CRM: Real Costs, Features, and What Actually Fits in 2026 Last updated: August 2026 The top pipedrive vs hubspot are Pipedrive (best for simple sales teams, From $14 to $79 per month), HubSpot (richest built-in features, From $0 to $75 per month), Miniloop (custom CRM for high spend, flexible deployments). In 2026, high CRM costs and workflow complexity have become common headaches for sales and operations teams. While Pipedrive and HubSpot remain dominant mid-market players, buyer expectations have shifted. Teams now want systems tailored to their processes and clear cost predictability. New options like custom CRM platforms are changing the math for companies with sizable CRM budgets. Which CRM type actually fits: Off-the-shelf or custom? Most companies compare Pipedrive and HubSpot by price and feature lists, but selecting the right CRM goes beyond basic comparisons. To make a decision that actually fits your organization, consider these factors: Workflow Fit: Off-the-shelf CRMs like Pipedrive and HubSpot are ideal if your team’s sales or support process closely matches industry-standard pipelines and you do not anticipate frequent changes. However, if your workflow involves specialized steps, multi-stage approvals, or needs to reflect strict regulatory requirements, a custom CRM is far more effective because it can be molded to your actual operations. Cost Predictability: Off-the-shelf solutions have recurring per-user costs and may introduce price increases as your user base grows or your process complexity requires higher tiers or paid add-ons. Custom CRMs require higher initial investment for setup and migration, but stabilize ongoing costs, especially valuable for large or fast-growing teams. Customization and Control: If you need to integrate deeply with in-house systems, maintain strict data residency, or enforce unique business logic, a custom CRM is the only route that won’t require continuous workarounds and shifting to spreadsheets or side tools. Off-the-shelf products generally offer only minor tweaks and depend on vendor roadmaps for major enhancements. Actionable Guidance: Small or early-stage teams with standard sales cycles and a need to launch quickly should opt for off-the-shelf CRMs like Pipedrive or HubSpot on the most appropriate tier. For larger organizations, those with high CRM spending, or those encountering repeated limitations in workflow or data requirements, investing in a custom-built CRM can provide a closer fit and more predictable long-term TCO. It’s smart to routinely evaluate your cost structure and admin time. If license and workaround costs begin to rival those for a custom solution, it’s time to reconsider your approach. CRM options at a glance: Pipedrive, HubSpot, and custom platforms Pipedrive is the pick for teams that want a simple, sales-focused CRM at lower price points, while HubSpot brings a full marketing and sales platform, though at a higher cost and complexity. Custom CRMs like Miniloop serve companies that need workflows tailored exactly to their business, offering infrastructure independence and long-term cost advantages by eliminating per-seat fees. Pipedrive is built for straightforward sales pipeline management. Priced from $14 to $79 per month, it stands out for its ease of use, quick setup, and focus on making sales activities more efficient. Sales teams or small businesses looking to get up and running quickly gravitate toward Pipedrive for its intuitive interface and no-nonsense workflow. However, it offers limited flexibility for teams with specialized or changing processes, and customizing beyond baked-in functionality usually requires external tools or workarounds. For organizations that mainly care about lead tracking, forecasting, and activity management, not broader marketing automation, Pipedrive is a cost-effective choice. For a deeper dive on how its pricing compares, see our Pipedrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and Comparative Analysis . HubSpot offers a much broader CRM suite, including sales, marketing, customer service, and even website management, with pricing from $0 to $75 per month (on published tiers). HubSpot is a fit for businesses wanting an all-in-one solution with extensive integrations and marketing features, such as campaign automation and content management. This power comes with a higher price tag as teams grow or require advanced features. And a steeper learning curve given the platform's depth. For companies with dedicated marketing functions or those who plan to scale to multi-channel campaigns, HubSpot often makes the shortlist. However, technical customization can be limited, and costs can increase quickly for larger teams or advanced needs. For more on HubSpot's position among enterprise CRMs, see our HubSpot vs Salesforce (2026): Pricing, Features, Which CRM Is Better . Custom CRM solutions such as Miniloop are designed for businesses that outgrow the limits of off-the-shelf software. These platforms are crafted around a company’s real workflow, not generic templates, offering data migration, a choice of where data is hosted, and crucially. No per-seat licensing fees. The up-front investment and development cycles can be significant compared to SaaS CRMs, but they make sense for teams spending around $50,000 a year or more on CRM tools, or those needing data control, specialized processes, or integration with in-house systems. Over time, custom CRMs can deliver major cost reductions, Miniloop positions itself as enabling teams to reduce CRM costs by 5x to significantly, by matching exact requirements and allowing control over infrastructure. Which path works best depends on your team’s size, annual spend, and process complexity. Small to midsize sales-driven teams benefit most from Pipedrive’s streamlined approach; HubSpot is attractive where marketing and sales operations merge on a single platform and the budget allows for it; while custom CRMs are the right move for larger organizations demanding workflow flexibility, data sovereignty, and a predictable long-term cost structure. Each model solves a distinct set of problems. Selecting the right one hinges on your tolerance for upfront investment, how rigid your workflows are, and whether long-term ownership costs weigh more than immediate convenience. Pipedrive vs HubSpot vs custom CRM: feature and integration comparison table Comparing Pipedrive, HubSpot, and custom CRM solutions side by side, pricing structure and flexibility vary dramatically. Pipedrive and HubSpot rely on per-seat pricing, with basic plans starting at $14 and $0 per month, respectively, but often escalate with users and features. Both offer user-friendly integrations, Pipedrive lists 500+ apps, while HubSpot includes a broad range of business tools, yet workflow customization is limited by the platform’s core design. A custom CRM, such as one developed by Miniloop, stands apart by offering flat-rate pricing with no per-seat fees, dynamic workflow design tailored to a business’s exact needs, and options for hosting on managed or client infrastructure. For teams scaling beyond “out-of-the-box” CRM limitations or managing complex migration from legacy systems, these differences become central to long-term cost and operational fit. Here’s a direct comparison of core features, integrations, and cost models for each: Platform Monthly/Annual Cost Structure Pipeline & Workflow Customization Integrations Available Data Migration Support Long-Term Scaling & Hidden Costs Pipedrive $14–$79/user/month Custom fields, pipeline stages; within platform limits 500+ integrations via app marketplace Guided migration tools Per-seat fees scale rapidly with team size; feature upgrades may require higher plans HubSpot $0–$75/user/month (Sales Hub) Workflow automation, customization guided by plan; constrained flexibility Broad business tool integrations; complexity increases with stack Assisted onboarding and migration Freemium tier limited; costs increase with features/users/add-ons Custom CRM (e.g., Miniloop) Flat-rate, no per-seat fees; pay for custom development/features Fully tailored workflows, infrastructure-independent Built-to-spec (as needed for client); not limited by preset app store Full migration from legacy CRMs, handled case-by-case Predictable costs for large teams; avoids per-user escalation; owned data and infra A custom CRM approach eliminates recurring per-seat fees, making it best suited for organizations with large teams or intricate processes unsatisfied by mainstream options. Meanwhile, Pipedrive excels for straightforward sales teams prioritizing quick setup and transparency, and HubSpot works for businesses seeking broad integrations and can handle a steeper learning curve. For more detail on pricing breakdowns, see Pipedrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and Comparative Analysis or compare major platforms in depth at HubSpot vs Salesforce (2026): Pricing, Features, Which CRM Is Better . Ditch your expensive CRM subscription Get a custom CRM designed for your workflow at a fraction of the price. Talk to our team to get a fixed quote. Book a call Pricing breakdown: Upfront, recurring, and hidden costs Pipedrive’s real cost runs far higher than the $14 to $79 per month headline because every user and add-on feature adds to your recurring bill; HubSpot’s stated $0 to $75 per month tiers climb quickly as you add seats and essential upgrades. Custom CRM solutions typically bring larger up-front costs for build and migration, but can structure ongoing fees without per-seat licensing, shifting the cost curve for teams scaling beyond a few users. Both Pipedrive and HubSpot highlight entry-level pricing: Pipedrive starts at $14/month, and HubSpot touts its free tier. In reality, neither option covers the needs of a typical midsize sales or support team at that base price. Critical functions, like advanced reporting, e-signatures, or sales automation triggers, require moving to higher plans ($79/month for Pipedrive’s top tier, $75/month for HubSpot’s Sales Hub Pro) or subscribing to add-ons. Every new team member increases total CRM cost, typical for models billing per seat. For a growing sales org, this means a price tag that rises with every new hire, as detailed in our Pipedrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and Comparative Analysis . HubSpot’s broad feature range comes with its own cost tiers and volume-based add-ons (marketing contacts, integrations, API access), leading many teams to face substantial unplanned expenses as needs change. These recurring per-seat and usage-based fees might feel manageable at first, but they compound rapidly as you scale. Picture a 15-person sales team: their monthly “headline” costs more than double when all necessary functionality and access are factored in, forcing a choice between extra spend and workflow compromises. Many teams also underestimate the one-off costs of switching CRMs down the road. Data migration, integration work, and staff retraining can create both direct expenses and weeks of productivity loss. Custom CRM platforms, such as Miniloop, invert many of these cost assumptions. The up-front investment is significant, covering requirements-gathering, build, migration, and configuration, but ongoing spend isn’t dictated by headcount. Organizations pay for custom-fit workflows and agreed-upon infrastructure. Without the ballooning monthly fees for each new user. Decision-makers focused on long-term total cost of ownership weigh larger initial outlay against predictable, often lower, ongoing spend. The real “price” of a CRM goes beyond simple subscription tiers. Teams quickly discover that headline rates rarely match monthly outlay at scale, especially once advanced features, integrations, and inevitable growth are factored in. Over several years, the gap between SaaS CRM and custom solutions can widen dramatically, especially for companies at or above the $50,000/year CRM spend threshold. Careful planning around both up-front and recurring costs is essential for avoiding financial surprises and “lock-in” pain as the company evolves. For deeper breakdowns of tradeoffs in tools like HubSpot, see HubSpot vs Salesforce (2026): Pricing, Features, Which CRM Is Better . Workflow fit: Where standard CRMs hit a wall Pipedrive and HubSpot both structure their CRMs around a set of default pipeline models and standardized sales stages, which work well for straightforward sales teams but often struggle to accommodate businesses with unusual approval steps, cross-team handoffs, or non-linear processes. While both platforms offer some customization, like editable stages and custom fields, there are real limits. When company logic falls outside their built-in workflows, teams are frequently forced into manual workarounds that add friction, increase risk, and undermine data integrity. Pipedrive’s pipelines are designed primarily for classic B2B sales cycles: leads move from qualification to proposal to close, using a series of stages such as “Contact Made,” “Meeting Scheduled,” and “Negotiation Started.” These pipelines can be duplicated or renamed, and custom fields allow for some flexibility in data capture, but the underlying logic remains a linear progression. Similarly, HubSpot employs deal pipelines that allow users to create custom properties and stages, but underlying automations and reporting favor single-track processes. For nuanced workflows, like deals with nested approval requirements, multiple product lines each with their own routes, or regulatory compliance records. These systems can only stretch so far before friction builds. Customization in both tools typically means adding custom fields, defining pipeline names, or building basic automation with the platform’s native builder. HubSpot’s marketplace offers integrations for more complex requirements, but plugging multiple point solutions together often introduces yet another layer of manual oversight. Pipedrive also supports over 500 integrations and customizable reports, but truly unique logic, like multi-level approvals that trigger based on changing business rules, or specialized audit trails for compliance. Often requires cumbersome Zapier chains, third-party add-ons, or spreadsheet workarounds. These compensations are fragile, difficult to scale, and can break with any change to the underlying system. Picture a growth-stage company whose business depends on coordinating internal approvals across finance, legal, and product before every high-value deal. In Pipedrive or HubSpot, such a team typically resorts to tracking stages through color codes, external checklists, or by creating parallel pipelines. None of which are natively enforced or reportable. Over time, these workarounds lead to inconsistent data and accountability gaps. For organizations with strict compliance mandates or those needing infrastructure control due to data sovereignty, the limitations are even sharper. Standard CRMs rely on the vendor’s cloud; options to host the system on your own infrastructure or implement custom security protocols are limited or nonexistent. A custom CRM, designed specifically around a team’s actual workflow, avoids these bottlenecks. By tailoring both the data model and the user experience, it ensures approvals, data collection, and process enforcement match exactly what the business needs. This control is essential not just for operational efficiency, but for companies that require data ownership or must demonstrate compliance to auditors and regulators. Domains where out-of-the-box CRMs often fall short. For a deeper look at how these limitations play out in competitive B2B environments, see our guide on Best B2B Sales Software in 2026: A Practical Guide for Lean GTM Teams . Integrations and extensibility: Limits of plug-and-play CRMs Pipedrive advertises over 500 integrations out-of-the-box, covering essentials like email, calendars, and marketing tools, while HubSpot supports hundreds of native and third-party connections alongside open API access for advanced customizations. These plug-and-play options make both platforms attractive for companies using popular apps, but integrating beyond well-supported tools often requires manual setup, middleware, or workarounds, which can introduce friction and ongoing maintenance. In detail, Pipedrive’s integration library spans categories such as communication (Slack, Zoom), document management (Google Drive, DocuSign), and lead capture (Mailchimp, Intercom). For most sales teams operating in standard SaaS environments, these connections work smoothly and can be activated with a few clicks. However, deeper automation, like syncing with industry-specific tools or bespoke back-office systems, may require third-party platforms (Zapier, Make), limited custom fields, or repeated exports and imports to bridge gaps. Workarounds can pile up quickly, and unique process steps may remain outside the CRM’s integration scope. For more about Pipedrive’s plans and integration tiers, see Pipedrive Pricing 2026 . HubSpot goes further with built-in connections across its wider suite (marketing, sales, service tools), offering end-to-end visibility if you commit to its ecosystem. The HubSpot API makes advanced integrations possible, supporting custom apps and automations. But API use demands technical resources, often requiring a developer or IT support, to keep things running and secure. As needs become more specialized, even HubSpot users may find limitations, especially when integrating with uncommon or internally-developed platforms. Going beyond these models, a custom CRM enables full control over integrations. With custom development, virtually any internal or external tool can connect, and data can reside according to company policies. Avoiding vendor-imposed silos. However, this flexibility comes with its own risk: integration projects require ongoing development attention, and the burden for updates or troubleshooting falls to your technical team or vendor. Unlike SaaS CRMs that automate updates, a custom setup means each new tool or system change could require new work. For organizations demanding deep customization and workflow alignment, this degree of extensibility is both a main benefit and a core responsibility. One that standard plug-and-play platforms can’t replicate, but which also comes without the safety net of a mass-market app library. For teams evaluating integration needs as part of their CRM search, it’s crucial to weigh the tradeoff between immediate app compatibility and the long-term demand for unique workflows. Those with conventional stacks may do fine within Pipedrive’s or HubSpot’s ecosystem; those with niche needs or aggressive internal system development should factor in the scope and resources required for reliable custom integrations. User experience and adoption: Simplicity vs. flexibility Pipedrive is renowned for its direct user experience and rapid onboarding, making it easy for sales teams to get started with minimal training; HubSpot, by contrast, offers a broader feature set but often introduces more complexity and a steeper learning curve. Custom CRM platforms handle onboarding differently. Typically involving a more guided, consultative setup period where workflows are designed around the team’s actual processes, but requiring more upfront time and coordination before users are hands-on. Pipedrive’s setup appeals to smaller and mid-sized teams that need to start tracking deals and contacts quickly. Its interface is streamlined, helping users get value without feeling overwhelmed. Most fields and views are customizable, but options remain intentionally limited to keep things simple. As teams grow, this can become a double-edged sword: adoption stays high while the demands of more nuanced workflows can reveal the platform’s inflexibility. HubSpot, meanwhile, offers a dense ecosystem of features and integrations spanning sales, marketing, and even support. This breadth gives growing or cross-functional teams much more power and automation, but navigating its configuration options and training users becomes a significant project in itself. Many encounter friction finding the features they need day-to-day, especially as their requirements expand. This theme recurs in deeper verticals like HubSpot vs Salesforce . Custom CRM onboarding starts very differently. Instead of users adapting to a pre-set structure, the CRM is shaped around the team’s language, stages, and unique needs. Often via workshops, iterative feedback, and direct migration of historical data. Users might have a slightly longer ramp-up, but ultimately face less daily friction, as the workflow fits what they actually do. Adoption is driven by relevance: the system reflects how people already work, rather than asking them to learn unfamiliar terminology or navigate unused modules. Support channels also differ. Pipedrive provides in-app chat and a self-serve knowledge base focused on quick fixes, which suits transactional questions but leaves little room for personalized onboarding. HubSpot offers a range of support, from community forums to premium onboarding services and live reps, but escalating an issue through layers of documentation and generic channels can still slow down resolution for busy teams. With custom CRMs, support is typically more hands-on and specialized. Teams work directly with those who built or tailored the system, allowing for deeper troubleshooting and ongoing tweaks as processes evolve. For teams weighing their options, the core tradeoff is clear: Pipedrive’s simplicity makes daily use easy but may frustrate as business complexity increases. HubSpot scales further but can burden users with complexity and extra features. Custom CRM solutions involve more commitment up front, yet return that investment with workflow-aligned simplicity and direct access to specialized support as the company grows. For deep dives into pricing and tradeoffs, Pipedrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and Comparative Analysis provides a granular breakdown. Long-term costs: Predictability vs creeping expenses Long-term CRM costs are far less predictable than many teams expect. Traditional platforms like Pipedrive and HubSpot appear affordable at first, but total spending rises sharply as user counts increase and workflows evolve, often making budgeting a challenge. By contrast, a custom CRM solution offers more control over costs, with stable long-term pricing and a structure that avoids per-seat fees entirely. Pipedrive and HubSpot both use subscription models where costs scale directly with the number of users. Pipedrive’s pricing ranges from $14 to $79 per user per month, while HubSpot charges from $0 to $75 per user per month, depending on the tier and features required. At first, this seems simple for annual budgeting, but as companies grow, new hires and cross-functional access needs can quickly inflate the total bill. When teams reorganize or add new roles, adding even a handful of users immediately increases recurring expenses, especially at higher tiers where advanced features are only available above a certain seat count. Workflow changes and new integration needs also drive incremental costs. For example, adding custom fields or automation in Pipedrive often requires upgrading to higher-priced tiers. HubSpot is known for including key CRM features only within premium packages, making “sticker shock” common when a business tries to adapt its CRM to new requirements. These variables, user growth, required integrations, expanded use cases, accumulate into an unpredictable cost trajectory. For a detailed breakdown of how these hidden increases happen, see Pipedrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and Comparative Analysis . Custom CRM solutions, by design, break this cycle. With no per-seat pricing and a cost structure based on the actual features and support a business needs, investment is more predictable year over year. Teams that outgrow off-the-shelf CRM platforms don’t face sudden fee spikes when onboarding new departments or making process changes, since their CRM is tailored and scaled to their workflow upfront. This ownership model aligns CRM costs with business priorities rather than vendor tiers, making it a preferred path for companies seeking long-term budgeting reliability. Custom CRMs also offer added stability for businesses that require data independence or infrastructure control, ensuring expenses stay aligned with usage rather than arbitrary limits. For businesses with complex processes or fast-changing teams, this difference can mean the gap between a CRM acting as a stable operational backbone versus an ongoing source of budgeting surprises. Readers comparing CRMs should pay close attention to how user additions, workflow modifications, and integration requirements translate into real long-term costs, especially as they plan for future growth. When is a custom CRM actually the smarter move? For teams spending $50,000 a year or more on CRM subscriptions, dealing with rigid workflows, or struggling with complex integrations, moving to a custom CRM often becomes the smarter investment. The major triggers are escalating license fees, increasing workaround-related friction, and the inability of off-the-shelf solutions to mesh with unique processes or deep data needs. Signs that the time and budget spent retrofitting standard platforms could be better invested in a system built for your organization from the ground up. Costs alone can tip the scale. When per-seat fees for platforms like HubSpot ($0–$75/month per user) or Pipedrive ($14–$79/month per user) begin compounding across departments, custom CRM solutions that eliminate licensing bloat and charge only for the features you actually use offer a path to reducing recurring expenses by a factor of five or ten. This appeals especially to businesses with mature sales operations, complex approval chains, or integration-heavy stacks where every new process demands yet another workaround or third-party add-on. Operational warning signs generally make themselves known through persistent pain points. These include frequent complaints about CRM limitations, growing shadow IT (teams building external spreadsheets or tools to compensate for CRM gaps), or mounting integration costs as business requirements shift beyond what plug-and-play platforms can handle. If standard CRMs force your team into repeated workarounds, or if you see bottlenecks that can’t be resolved through available settings and add-ons, it’s a strong indicator that off-the-shelf options are holding your team back. Articles like Best B2B Sales Software in 2026: A Practical Guide for Lean GTM Teams provide more perspective on when specialized needs eclipse standard functionality. The process of moving to a custom CRM is different from deploying a prepackaged tool. Instead of picking modules from a menu, expect a tailored build: interviewing stakeholders, mapping your real workflows, and collaborating on interfaces that match your team’s habits. Data migration is a critical step, ensuring continuity even when moving from legacy systems. A strong custom CRM partner will also give you a choice in hosting, letting you control your data on your infrastructure or use managed servers, alongside hands-on support from people, not just documentation or bots. This degree of fit and ownership isn’t possible with off-the-shelf CRMs, which are designed to serve the median customer, not the unique contours of your business. Automate CRM busywork instead of building around it Pipedrive, HubSpot, and similar CRMs provide the essentials for sales tracking, contact management, and reporting. But the day-to-day realities of CRM use extend far beyond lead records and pipelines. The tools above stop short when it comes to the repetitive, manual tasks that slow down teams: onboarding new users, updating role hierarchies, refining approval flows, and reworking existing workflows as your business evolves. These are the tasks that pile up, increase friction, and ultimately drive staff to bend the system with manual workarounds. Miniloop steps in to handle what standard CRMs treat as "external" or "manual" needs, so recurring CRM maintenance and admin doesn't consume your schedule. With Miniloop, you get: A custom CRM designed around your team’s unique workflow, not the other way around Full data migration from your legacy CRM platform, including structure, records, and configuration Flexible hosting: run on Miniloop-managed servers or fully own the infrastructure on your terms No per-seat licensing fees. Pay only for what you actually need, no matter how your team changes Dedicated human and AI support to resolve edge cases, operational gaps, and evolving requirements Miniloop is designed for mid-sized and enterprise organizations where CRM upkeep, including routine onboarding and complex admin, is a costly distraction. Instead of workarounds and accumulating workaround fatigue, your team gets tailored workflows and maintenance handled by a partner who understands and adapts to your requirements as you scale. Ready to see how a CRM can support your business, instead of creating extra work? Try Miniloop to get started. Have questions about your specific workflows or infrastructure needs? Get in touch . Who should pick Pipedrive, HubSpot, or custom CRM in 2026? Pipedrive is the clear pick for small, sales-focused teams with straightforward processes and a need to keep monthly costs low. HubSpot is the better fit for midsize or large teams that require an extensive set of built-in features and integrations, trading higher price and complexity for broader capabilities. Custom CRM solutions become the obvious choice for companies managing intricate workflows, strict compliance, or high CRM spending, especially those wanting to avoid paying per-user fees and seeking long-term infrastructure control. For lean sales organizations or startups with standard deal stages and a tight budget, Pipedrive stands out. It offers unlimited sales pipelines, customizable fields, and an easy learning curve, which covers most common sales use cases without introducing unnecessary overhead. Teams that don’t need marketing automation or granular user permissions will typically get all the essentials for a starting price of $14 per month, making it a favorite among teams that value simplicity over a feature-packed environment. For a deeper dive on cost structure, see Pipedrive Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs, and Comparative Analysis . When sales and marketing must work closely together, or your business model requires a suite of automation, reporting, and third-party integrations, HubSpot is engineered for that environment. Its stack delivers comprehensive lead management, robust automation, and integrations with a wide array of business tools, but this comes with a steeper price, from $0 to $75 per month, and a much higher learning curve. Large teams may find the investment worthwhile, though the system’s depth can slow down onboarding and configuration, a key critique surfaced in HubSpot vs Salesforce (2026): Pricing, Features, Which CRM Is Better . Teams handling complex deal structures, heavy compliance obligations, or spending $50,000 or more annually on CRM platforms should strongly consider a custom CRM. Solutions like Miniloop uniquely cater to organizations needing tailored workflows, direct data ownership, and infrastructure independence. Custom CRM routes can cut long-term costs significantly by eliminating per-seat licensing fees and focusing only on what your business actually needs, rather than paying for underutilized features or workarounds. This is especially relevant when scaling, navigating mergers, or adapting systems to unique industry specifics that boxed CRMs can’t flexibly support. Pipedrive is typically favored by small businesses due to its focus on straightforward sales processes, lower base prices, and quick setup. Its interface is intuitive for teams looking to track leads and activities without much customization or extra features. HubSpot offers more depth, including marketing automation and customer service tools, but this comes at the cost of greater complexity and higher overall expenses as feature needs expand. For small businesses needing only essential CRM capabilities, Pipedrive is often the simpler and more budget-friendly choice. If broader functionalities or marketing tools are critical, HubSpot may be worth the extra investment. What are the real annual costs after upgrades and user growth? The sticker price for CRMs like Pipedrive and HubSpot can be misleading since costs increase significantly as your team grows or requires advanced features. Per-seat fees, mandatory add-ons, and required plan upgrades all add up, pushing annual spend much higher than initial estimates, especially for companies scaling past a handful of users. It's common for mid-sized teams to see real costs multiply several times over their initial budget. Custom CRM platforms, such as Miniloop, take a different approach by eliminating per-seat licensing, offering more predictable and potentially much lower long-term costs for larger or rapidly growing organizations. How hard is it to switch from HubSpot or Pipedrive to a custom CRM? Migrating from an off-the-shelf CRM to a custom solution often involves extracting existing data, reformatting it, and mapping it to the new system's structure. The complexity depends on the volume of data and the number of custom fields or workflows in your old CRM. Some custom CRM providers, including Miniloop, specialize in full data migration and support to reduce disruption. While setup requires more planning than a plug-and-play tool, the tradeoff is a solution tailored to your process and data needs. Does a custom CRM like Miniloop work for marketing teams too? A custom CRM can be designed to fit the workflows of marketing teams as well as sales and operations. The main advantage is that it can be tailored around specific marketing processes, such as campaign tracking, segmentation, or content workflows, without being limited by generic features. Miniloop, for example, is built for organizations that need customized workflows, meaning it can address the needs of both sales and marketing teams when required. This flexibility can be particularly valuable for companies where standard CRM tools fall short. Which platform is easiest to integrate with other business tools? Off-the-shelf CRMs like HubSpot typically offer extensive libraries of prebuilt integrations, especially for popular SaaS products, making them easier to connect out-of-the-box. Pipedrive also provides a wide range of integrations, though with a narrower focus on sales and productivity apps. Custom CRMs offer the most flexibility for integrating with unique or legacy systems, but may require more upfront development work. The best choice depends on whether your integration needs are standard (favoring Pipedrive or HubSpot) or highly specific (favoring a custom CRM). How do per-seat fees actually impact long-term CRM costs? Per-seat licensing means your CRM costs grow with your team. Each additional user increases the monthly or annual bill, often necessitating more expensive plan tiers as you scale. This can result in unexpectedly high expenses over time, especially for organizations with frequent onboarding or large teams across departments. For companies with stable or shrinking headcounts, this may be manageable, but for those planning to grow, costs can escalate quickly. Custom CRM solutions like Miniloop remove per-seat fees, offering a more stable long-term cost structure. What’s the migration process like for moving all our CRM data? Migrating CRM data involves exporting information such as contacts, deals, notes, and historical activity from your old system, then importing and aligning it with the new platform. The process may require data cleaning, field mapping, and validation to ensure nothing is lost or miscategorized. Many custom CRM providers assist with or manage this process, minimizing risk and downtime. The timeline depends on data complexity and the level of customization required in the new system. Can a custom CRM be owned outright or does it require ongoing licensing? Some custom CRMs can be structured for outright ownership, especially if they are hosted on your own infrastructure and do not involve seat-based fees or proprietary cloud dependencies. Others may charge for ongoing support, updates, or managed hosting, but these costs are often not tied to the number of users. Miniloop allows businesses to avoid per-seat licensing and gives flexibility in hosting, supporting data ownership and infrastructure independence. This can appeal to organizations wanting control over both cost and technology choices. Where do Pipedrive and HubSpot fall short for teams with unique workflows? These platforms excel at serving common sales and marketing use cases but can struggle when a business’s processes fall outside the typical mold. Customization options are often limited to predefined fields, automation, and integrations, making more complex or niche workflows difficult to implement without workarounds. Teams may find themselves hacking together solutions or relying on costly third-party tools to bridge gaps. Custom CRMs are designed specifically to address these kinds of requirements, allowing for workflows and structures that match your business exactly. How long does it really take to build and onboard a custom CRM? The timeline for building and onboarding a custom CRM is highly dependent on the complexity of your requirements and the scope of data migration. While basic setups can be achieved in a few weeks, more complex, highly-tailored platforms may take several months from initial planning to full deployment. This process includes discovery, system design, migration, testing, and team training. The upfront investment in time is greater than with off-the-shelf CRMs, but it can greatly improve fit and long-term efficiency for large or specialized teams.

title: Mike Mendoza Joins eXp Realty Luxury
summary: Former MLB player Mike Mendoza joins eXp Realty Luxury after 29 years at Keller Williams. Discover his team's next move in real estate today!
body_text: Mendoza, who built Keller Williams’ Northwest Region into 30 Market Centers and 3,500+ agents, brings his Arizona-based family team to eXp after 29 years. BELLINGHAM, Washington, August 4, 2026 — eXp Realty®, the most agent-centric™ real estate brokerage on the planet and the core subsidiary of AGNT, Inc. (Nasdaq: AGNT), today announced that former Major League Baseball player and longtime real estate leader Mike Mendoza has joined eXp Realty Luxury after 29 years with Keller Williams. Mendoza brings more than four decades of real estate experience and approximately 6,500 transactions to his career. As founder and former Operating Principal of Keller Williams Northwest Region, he grew the company’s footprint across Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Alaska into a network of 30 Market Centers and more than 3,500 agents. “Mike’s career is what happens when talent, discipline and an entrepreneurial mindset come together,” said Leo Pareja, CEO of eXp Realty. “His decision to choose eXp after 29 years speaks volumes about where experienced leaders see the strongest opportunities for their teams and families. We are proud to welcome Mike, Jude, Josh and the entire Mendoza Team to eXp.” Mendoza was introduced to eXp by longtime real estate friends Lou Ronayne and Gene Frederick. As he learned more about the company, he saw a platform equipped to help his family and team evolve alongside a rapidly changing industry. “There is more opportunity for me, my son Josh, and the rest of our team with eXp,” Mendoza said. “It’s a cutting-edge company with technology that is also focused on agent support. I like the forward-looking mentality to help agents grow and succeed in a constantly shifting industry.” Joining Mendoza at eXp are his wife and business partner, Jude Mendoza; his son, Josh Mendoza; and agents Rob Castellini, Cheryl Kvasnicka, Megan Bradley, Brad Turk and Taylor Turk. Together, the Ahwatukee-based Mendoza Team serves residential and luxury clients throughout Phoenix, the Valley and surrounding metropolitan areas. Mendoza spent decades building offices and opportunities for thousands of agents. Now, he’s channeling that same focus into his own family’s team. About AGNT, Inc. (AGNT) Built by Agents. Built for Agents. AGNT, Inc. (Nasdaq: AGNT) is the global parent company of eXp Realty®, the most agent-centric™ real estate brokerage on the planet, NextHome, Inc., an award-winning national real estate franchise, FrameVR.io, a virtual collaboration platform, and SUCCESS® Enterprises, a leading personal development and media brand for entrepreneurs. Together, the AGNT platform provides a world-class multi-model operating system empowering independent agents, franchise owners, and team leaders across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Asia Pacific, and South Africa. As a publicly traded company, AGNT prioritizes transparency, innovation, and long-term value for agents, franchise owners, staff, and shareholders. title: Vivani Medical Announces Successful Dosing of All Participants in SLIM-1, a Phase 1 Trial Evaluating NPM-139, a Miniature, Ultra Long-Acting Semaglutide Implant for Chronic Weight Management
summary: Dosing of the first participant commenced ahead of schedule and was rapidly followed by initial dosing in all trial participants. SLIM-1™ trial…...
body_text: Vivani Medical Announces Successful Dosing of All Participants in SLIM-1, a Phase 1 Trial Evaluating NPM-139, a Miniature, Ultra Long-Acting Semaglutide Implant for Chronic Weight Management August 06, 2026 8:00am EDT Download as PDF Dosing of the first participant commenced ahead of schedule and was rapidly followed by initial dosing in all trial participants. SLIM-1 ™ trial is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled clinical trial design to characterize the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of NPM-139 including a Wegovy® (semaglutide injection) group. Top-line data from the 20-participant trial is expected in November of 2026. ALAMEDA, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Vivani Medical, Inc. (Nasdaq: VANI) today announced full enrollment and successful initial dosing of all participants in its SLIM-1™ Phase 1 trial for NPM-139, a miniature, subdermal semaglutide implant being designed to provide six- to twelve-months of continuous drug delivery utilizing our proprietary NanoPortal™ technology. The trial of 20 GLP-1 naïve participants in Australia includes low-doses of NPM-139 and Wegovy® to assess safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics. Changes in weight will be measured. “Dosing of the first 10 participants occurred on July 29, ahead of schedule. The remaining 10 participants were dosed one week later. All insertion procedures were completed successfully without any issues. Expeditious full enrollment of SLIM-1 trial participants highlights our commitment to rapidly advance the development of our innovative GLP-1 product candidates in chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes,” said Adam Mendelsohn, Ph.D., CEO of Vivani Medical. “We look forward to sharing top-line SLIM-1 clinical data later this year which we anticipate will pave the way for initiation of a Phase 2 dose-ranging trial in 2027.” This milestone follows NPM-139 preclinical studies demonstrating sustainable 20% weight reduction in animal models and a July 2026 agreement with Novo Nordisk to evaluate NPM-139 and Vivani’s proprietary NanoPortal implant technology. In addition to NPM-139’s primary aim to improve convenience, medication adherence and tolerability, NanoPortal implants are uniquely designed to enable infrequent administration (six months or longer) and the ability to rapidly reverse GLP-1 drug exposure when cessation of therapy is needed or desired. Reversibility can be an important clinical consideration in certain situations, including when a woman becomes pregnant or when patients undergoing surgery have an increased aspiration risk. About SLIM-1 SLIM-1 is an open-label, active-controlled trial evaluating a low-dose NPM-139 (semaglutide implant) given to 10 participants, and the starting dose of Wegovy (0.25mg/week semaglutide injection) also given to 10 participants, over a four-week duration. The trial is designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetic profile in overweight or obese participants who are otherwise healthy. Top-line results from SLIM-1 are expected to be available in November. About Vivani Medical, Inc. Leveraging its proprietary NanoPortal™ platform, Vivani develops miniature, biopharmaceutical implants designed to deliver drug molecules steadily over extended periods of time with the goal of guaranteeing adherence and improving patient tolerance to their medication. Vivani is developing a portfolio of GLP-1 based implants for metabolic diseases including obesity and type 2 diabetes. These NanoPortal implants are designed for once- or twice-yearly administration to provide patients with the opportunity to realize the full potential benefit of their medication by avoiding the numerous challenges associated with the daily or weekly administration of orals and injectables, including tolerability issues and loss of efficacy. Medication non-adherence occurs when patients do not take their medication as prescribed. This affects an alarming number of patients, approximately 50%, including those taking daily pills. title: Titan Mining Reports 57% Revenue Growth and Nearly 4x Adjusted EBITDA
summary: We are an Augusta Group company which produces zinc concentrate at its 100%-owned Empire State Mine located in New York state.
body_text: Titan Mining Reports 57% Revenue Growth and Nearly 4x Adjusted EBITDA View PDF U.S. Graphite Strategy Accelerates with Supply Agreements and U.S. Army Conditional Selection Gouverneur, NY, August 12, 2026 – Titan Mining Corporation ( NYSE-A:TII, TSX:TI ) (“Titan” or the “Company”), a U.S.-focused critical minerals producer and developer, today reported record financial performance for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Q2 2026 HIGHLIGHTS(1)(2) Operating and Financial Performance: Zinc production: 17.5 million payable pounds, up 13% year-over-year and up 23% from Q1 2026, ahead of the mine plan Revenue: $25.7 million, up 57% from Q2 2025 and up 31% from Q1 2026 — the Company’s highest quarterly revenue since Q4 2024 Adjusted EBITDA: $9.6 million, up 272% year-over-year and up 135% quarter-over-quarter; first-half Adjusted EBITDA of $13.6 million is on track for the $20 – $28 million full-year guidance(3) Net income: $5.4 million, or $0.06 per basic share, compared with $0.5 million in Q2 2025 Zinc price: Average provisional price of $1.57 per pound, up 7% from Q1 2026; spot zinc price has risen significantly since quarter-end, currently trading at a 4-year high near $1.70 per pound Cash costs(4): C1 cash costs of $0.88 per pound, down 15% from Q1 2026 and below the low end of the full-year guidance range of $0.93 – $1.01 per pound; AISC of $0.96 per pound, down 9% quarter-over-quarter and below the full-year guidance range of $1.07 – $1.17 per pound Cash flow: Operating cash flow before changes in non-cash working capital of $4.9 million, up 156% from Q1 2026 Balance sheet: Net debt of $12.8 million, down 47% from $24.2 million a year ago; well-positioned with available liquidity of $29.1 million and net working capital of $17.8 million at quarter-end Guidance reaffirmed: Remain on track for 2026 production of 62 – 66 million payable zinc pounds, C1 cash costs of $0.93 – $1.01 per pound and AISC of $1.07 – $1.17 per pound, with sustaining capital expenditures weighted toward the second half of the year Strategic and Corporate Developments: Historic U.S Army Support: Titan received Conditional Selection Notices for Enhanced Use Lease opportunities at two strategic defense installations under the U.S. Army's Strategic Capital Initiatives program and is finalizing Business Terms Agreements to build and operate the Kilbourne graphite purification plant on Army property. This federal support is in addition to the previously announced expression of financing interest of up to $120 million from EXIM Bank under its Make More in America program and existing financing for the Kilbourne feasibility study. Graphite Commercialization: Subsequent to quarter-end, Titan secured two customer agreements supporting commercialization of the Kilbourne Graphite Project—one conditional supply agreement with RHI Magnesita, a global leader in refractory products, following successful laboratory qualification and commencement of commercial-scale trials, and a non-binding LOI with a U.S. aerospace, defense and advanced industrial manufacturer, with customer qualification underway. Together, these agreements support Titan's strategy of building its commercial order book and advancing toward commercial production. Battery-Grade Graphite Confirmed: Titan announced positive results across its full processing chain, from ore concentration through battery-grade spherical graphite, confirming the Preliminary Economic Assessment design assumptions and supporting the ongoing Feasibility Study. Germanium Upside: Titan entered into a cooperation agreement with Teck Resources to evaluate germanium recovery from existing ESM process streams. District-wide sampling also confirmed widespread germanium enrichment, highlighting the potential for an incremental revenue stream alongside the existing zinc operation. Unless noted otherwise, all monetary figures are expressed in U.S. Dollars. C1 Cash Cost, All-In Sustaining Cost (“AISC”), Adjusted EBITDA and Net Debt are non-GAAP measures. Accordingly, these financial measures are not standardized financial measures under IFRS and might not be comparable to similar financial measures disclosed by other issuers. These financial measures have been calculated on a basis consistent with historical periods. Information explaining these non-GAAP measures is provided below under “Non-GAAP Performance Measures”. Estimated based on approximate current spot zinc pricing, assuming production and costs remain in line with guidance. Actual realized pricing and Adjusted EBITDA may vary based on operational and market conditions. C1 cash cost and AISC reported for Q1 2026 have been revised to align with the definitions outlined in the Non-GAAP Performance Measures section below and past practice, resulting in increases of $0.06 and $0.05 per pound, respectively, compared with the figures reported in Titan’s Q1 2026 MD&A dated May 12, 2026 Rita Adiani, President and Chief Executive Officer, commented: "Titan delivered a record quarter. Revenue grew 57% and Adjusted EBITDA nearly quadrupled year-over-year, reflecting the strength of our zinc operations. We have continued to advance our Kilbourne graphite project by securing two graphite customer agreements, validating Kilbourne and launching our commercial order book. Just as important, the balance sheet is materially stronger, providing flexibility to advance our strategic initiatives. Available liquidity stands at $29.1 million, and our zinc operation is generating cash flow to support growth. With a fully funded feasibility study and growing commercial momentum, Titan is well positioned to become a leading U.S. supplier of critical minerals to defense and industrial supply chains”. Net income before tax for Q2 2026 was $6.1 million, including a non-cash fair value gain of $2.7 million on derivative financial instruments measured at fair value through profit or loss under IFRS. For the six months ended June 30, 2026, the Company recorded a net loss before tax of $7.3 million, primarily reflecting a non-cash fair value loss of $10.5 million recognized for the six months ended June 30, 2026. Cash generated from operating activities, after changes in non-cash working capital, was $0.3 million during the quarter. For the first half of 2026, operating cash outflow was $1.8 million, reflecting continued investment in growth initiatives, including exploration, the graphite demonstration facility and the graphite feasibility study, which totaled $4.8 million during the quarter and $7.1 million for the first half. These growth initiatives were fully funded through equity and debt proceeds and are expensed under the Company's accounting policies. The Company ended the quarter with $29.1 million of available liquidity, comprising $13.3 million in cash and $15.8 million of undrawn EXIM facility capacity. ZINC OPERATIONS REVIEW Mining in Q2 2026 focused on the Mahler, New Fold and Mud Pond zones in the #4 mine. Recovery of high-grade pillars in Lower Mahler and longhole stoping in the Mud Pond Apron delivered above-target grades and tonnes, fully recovering the production shortfall caused by the first-quarter hoisting outage. Mining in the N2D zone remained temporarily suspended, with equipment redeployed to the higher-grade Mud Pond Apron; operations are expected to resume in the fourth quarter. Development was completed on the New Fold–Mahler connection, improving ventilation in the lower mining zones, while ramp development continued in New Fold and Upper Mahler. Capital projects advanced as planned, including the production shaft rail replacement, rehabilitation of the #2 shaft secondary egress, fine ore bin chute rebuild, and power expansion at Mud Pond. A 42-ton haul truck and mechanical bolter were delivered and are expected to be commissioned by year-end. GRAPHITE UPDATE During Q2 2026, the Kilbourne Graphite Project advanced across all key workstreams. The demonstration facility improved throughput and concentrate grade through process optimization and delivered its first large-volume shipment to a Tier 1 customer. The fully funded Feasibility Study for the proposed 40,000 tpa facility remains on schedule, with $5.3 million of the $20.7 million budget incurred as of June 30, 2026. Subsequent to quarter-end, Titan confirmed battery-grade graphite production across the full processing chain, validating the Preliminary Economic Assessment design assumptions. A construction decision remains targeted for early 2027, subject to Board approval, Feasibility Study results, permitting and financing. EXPLORATION UPDATE Zinc: Underground drilling totalled 9,100 feet across 19 holes, supporting exploration and definition programs at Mud Pond, Lower Mahler and New Fold. Surface Drilling also tested the Little York and Bend targets, with assay results pending. Planned drilling includes continued definition and long-range exploration at New Fold, and definition drilling at Upper Mahler beginning in August. Kilbourne Graphite Project: Drilling totalled 2,278 feet across seven holes, including infill and geotechnical drilling in support of the Feasibility Study. Hole KX26-080 intersected 2.8% Cg over 106.5 feet, including 3.3% Cg over 49.9 feet, with remaining assays pending. Field work has now shifted primarily to geotechnical activities supporting the Feasibility Study. Germanium: Titan completed a property-wide sampling program across six underground ore bodies and two historic tailings facilities, confirming district-wide germanium enrichment. The program is advancing to prioritization and recovery test work in parallel with ongoing mineralogical studies and the Teck cooperation agreement. Scientific and Technical Information The scientific and technical information contained in this news release related to the Company’s exploration activities and zinc operations has been reviewed and approved by Matthew Melnyk, CPG #11540, Vice President Exploration and Geology of Titan Mining Corp., a Qualified Person as defined by National Instrument 43-101 - Standards of Disclosure for Mineral Projects (“ NI 43-101 "). The scientific and technical information contained in this news release related to the Company’s germanium and graphite development has been reviewed and approved by Oliver Peters, MSc., P.Eng., who is a Qualified Person as defined by NI 43-101. Mr. Peters is independent of the Company. The Company believes that these performance measures are commonly used by certain investors, in conjunction with conventional GAAP measures, to enhance their understanding of the Company's performance. The Company uses these performance measures extensively in internal decision-making processes, including to assess how well ESM is performing and to assist in the assessment of the overall efficiency and effectiveness of the mine site management team. The tables below provide a reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable IFRS measures as contained within the Company's issued financial statements. C1 Cash Cost Per Payable Pound Sold C1 cash cost is a non-GAAP measure. C1 cash cost represents the cash cost incurred at each processing stage, from mining through to recoverable metal delivered to customers, including mine site operating and general and administrative costs, freight, treatment and refining charges. The C1 cash cost per payable pound sold is calculated by dividing the total C1 cash costs by payable pounds of metal sold. All-in Sustaining Costs AISC measures the estimated cash costs to produce a pound of payable zinc plus the estimated capital sustaining costs to maintain the mine and mill. This measure includes the C1 cash cost and capital sustaining costs divided by pounds of payable zinc sold. AISC does not include depreciation, depletion, amortization, reclamation and exploration expenses. title: The Best Cars for Tall People in 2026
summary: Searching for vehicles best suited for tall people? Keep reading to find out which cars, trucks, and SUVs best accommodate those with a higher stature, as recommended by the experts at CarGurus.
body_text: Finding the right car when you're taller than average can be a frustrating experience. A vehicle that looks spacious on the outside can feel surprisingly cramped once you're behind the wheel, with your head brushing the headliner and your knees jammed against the dashboard. The search for a comfortable fit isn't just about avoiding discomfort on short trips; it's about ensuring a safe and ergonomic driving position for your daily commute and long road trips. A proper fit means better visibility, less fatigue, and an overall more pleasant ownership experience. This guide is designed to help tall drivers find a vehicle that offers generous headroom and legroom without sacrificing practicality, technology, or style. We've selected a diverse range of options, from rugged SUVs with upright, boxy designs like the Ford Bronco Sport to comfortable and tech-forward sedans like the Genesis G80. Whether you need a family-hauling three-row SUV, an efficient commuter car, or even a high-performance coupe, this list proves that you don't have to compromise on your needs to find a car that fits your frame. The power-adjustable front seats and practical cabin storage help it function like a daily driver, and the trunk is legitimately useful at 14 cubic feet—about what you’d expect from a mainstream compact sedan. Even the rear seat can handle adults on shorter trips, which matters if you’re the tall friend who still ends up driving everyone. The main tall-person caveat is access: the deeply bolstered seats (and the carbon-fiber wedge found on the optional carbon bucket seats) can make getting in and out more of a maneuver than a simple slide-in, especially if you’re long-legged. Once underway, the tallish greenhouse and normal-sized pillars provide excellent sight lines, and iDrive 8’s mix of touchscreen and rotary controller keeps the tech easy to live with. Just keep in mind the mission here is speed—powered by a twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-six making 453 hp and 406 lb-ft of torque—so even in its calmer drive modes, the ride is notably stiff. The CarGurus Verdict: "To automotive enthusiasts, a sports car like the BMW M2 is special. The modern car market is marching away in multiple directions from the purist driving experience. The cabin also feels more modern than you’d expect for the money, with an available 12.3-inch digital instrument display (7 inches on the base S) and a 12.3-inch center touchscreen across the lineup—useful if you prefer clearer, larger on-screen text and controls. The trade-off is in the back seat. Rear-seat legroom runs tight compared with many compact sedan rivals, so if you routinely carry taller adults behind you, it’s smart to test your “me behind me” fit before buying. Up front, the Sentra stays focused on commuting rather than quick acceleration—its 2.0-liter four-cylinder makes 149 hp and 146 lb-ft of torque—while available driver assists like ProPilot Assist (SR/SL) can take some strain out of highway miles for larger drivers who value a relaxed, tech-forward ride. The CarGurus Verdict: "The 2026 Nissan Sentra is a stylish and safe compact sedan that delivers impressive technology at an attractive, affordable price. It’s not the most thrilling car in its segment (look to the Honda Civic or Mazda3 for that honor), but it nevertheless delivers premium, in-demand features." - Matt Smith Read our most recent Nissan Sentra review Search for Nissan Sentra See all 2020 Nissan Sentra $13,499 76,663 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Orlando, FL 2020 Nissan Sentra $10,986 76,962 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Jacksonville, FL 2021 Nissan Sentra $16,369 50,198 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Jacksonville, FL 2024 Nissan Sentra $16,289 55,139 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Highlands Ranch, CO 2021 Nissan Sentra $12,288 86,162 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Tampa, FL 2024 Nissan Sentra $15,622 44,634 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Fort Lauderdale, FL Midsize Cars Genesis G80 CarGurus expert rating : 8.2 out of 10 CarGurus user rating : 4.7 out of 5 Percentage of Good and Great Deals available on CarGurus : 29.2% Overall CarGurus rating : 4.3 out of 5 Pros Cons Excellent value for money Poor fuel economy Great ride quality Fairly pedestrian performance Premium interior materials Tall drivers who are tired of feeling perched on top of a car’s cabin will likely appreciate the G80’s easygoing, long-haul personality and the space that comes with its generous wheelbase. Headroom is good and there’s plenty of legroom front and back, and the front seats are set up for comfort on long commutes with standard luxury touches like a heated steering wheel and heated front and rear seats. If you move between drivers or like to fine-tune your position, the available Ergo-Motion driver’s seat is designed to adjust with drive modes, though the effect can be subtle. The 2025 refresh also brings a wide 27-inch OLED display for gauges and infotainment, which makes it easier to place navigation and key info in your sightline without squinting, and there are still physical dials for volume and temperature. For tall people, small cabin details matter on daily use: the G80 has lots of storage throughout the cabin, a big center console, and a padded insert between the seat and console so dropped items don’t vanish into the footwell. The trunk is an average 13.1 cubic-feet, but the pass-through is useful for longer gear, and the overall driving experience is tuned more for a smooth ride than for hustling—whether you choose the 2.5-liter turbo with 300 hp and 311 lb-ft of torque or the 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6 with 375 hp and 391 lb-ft of torque. Kia makes a front passenger seat height adjuster standard across the lineup (a small feature that can make a big difference for long legs), and in EX trim both front seats add 10-way power adjustment plus heating and ventilation. The cabin is generally roomy for legs, feet, and heads, and the supportive rear seat is comfortable for adults, helped by rear air vents that keep the back seat from feeling like an afterthought on longer drives. The K5’s refreshed interior tech can also make it easier to live with when you’re settled in and stretching out for a commute. The available 24-inch Panoramic Display combines the digital gauges and the infotainment screen in a wide, modern layout, and every K5 gets a 12.3-inch touchscreen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Just be aware that the touch-sensing, dual-action control panel for audio and climate can be distracting to use, especially if you’re trying to make quick adjustments from a relaxed driving position. For trips that demand luggage space, the trunk’s 15.6 cubic feet is a practical bonus, and the standard 191-hp 2.5-liter four-cylinder (182 lb-ft of torque) is adequate even if it doesn’t feel as punchy as the old turbo engine. The CarGurus Verdict: "Unfortunately, the 2025 Kia K5 still doesn’t offer a hybrid powertrain like its corporate cousin, the Hyundai Sonata, does. It’s also less enjoyable to drive, thanks to this year’s engine swap. However, the new tech impresses, the K5 remains stylish and comfortable, and it costs less than some rivals." - Christian Wardlaw Read our most recent Kia K5 review Search for Kia K5 See all 2022 Kia K5 $22,847 22,931 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Streetsboro, OH 2022 Kia K5 $19,990 41,336 miles No additional dealer fees Great Deal Omaha, NE 2021 Kia K5 $20,231 70,715 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Alamogordo, NM 2021 Kia K5 $16,679 105,797 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Waterloo, IA 2022 Kia K5 $15,340 133,669 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Minneapolis, MN 2021 Kia K5 $20,317 7,065 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Saint Cloud, MN Compact SUVs Ford Bronco Sport CarGurus expert rating : 7.8 out of 10 CarGurus user rating : 4.4 out of 5 Percentage of Good and Great Deals available on CarGurus : 33.9% Overall CarGurus rating : 4.5 out of 5 Pros Cons Great handling Excessive touchscreen controls Standard all-wheel drive Mediocre fuel economy Stylish design The 2025 Ford Bronco Sport’s upright shape pays off in headroom. Ford notes it has more first- and second-row headroom than off-road-leaning rivals like the Jeep Compass Trailhawk, Subaru Forester Wilderness, and Toyota RAV4 TRD Off-Road, and that extra vertical space helps make the driving position feel less cramped on longer trips. Up front, it also offers more first-row legroom than most of those competitors, which is a big deal for longer legs—plus the squared-off hood and tall glass make it easier to place the vehicle without hunching forward in the seat. Tall drivers who also need everyday usefulness will appreciate that the Bronco Sport’s off-road focus doesn’t come with a penalty in basic practicality: cargo space is 32.5 cu ft behind the rear seats and 65.2 cu ft with them folded on standard configurations (though some higher trims drop to 29.4/60.6 cu ft). Power comes from a 1.5-liter turbo three-cylinder with 180 hp and 200 lb-ft of torque or, in Badlands models, a 2.0-liter turbo four-cylinder with 250 hp and 280 lb-ft of torque, both with standard AWD; it stays comfortable and composed on-road even when equipped for dirt. For 2025, Sync 4 with a 13.2-inch touchscreen and a 12.3-inch digital cluster modernizes the cabin, though some common functions still rely heavily on the touchscreen, which may be a nuisance if you prefer simple, easy-to-reach physical controls. The driver gets 10-way power adjustment and supportive heated front seats, and the boxy shape helps the cabin feel open rather than pinched—useful if you’re broad-shouldered or simply don’t like low, sloping rooflines. Subaru’s new center console design for 2026 also improves day-to-day usability, with more practical storage for larger bottles and small items that otherwise end up in knee space. The Wilderness trim adds adventure-ready details without giving up the practical stuff tall people tend to appreciate in a compact SUV, including a roomy second row with good legroom, rear air vents, and charging ports. Cargo room is also solid for the segment at 27.5 cubic feet behind the rear seat and 69.1 cubic feet with the 60/40 rear seat folded, even with a full-size all-terrain spare stored under the load floor. Both are crucial, but the ideal balance depends on your body proportions. If you have a long torso, prioritize headroom to avoid hitting the headliner. If you have long legs, focus on legroom and a telescoping steering wheel that allows you to sit comfortably far from the pedals. The best approach is to test-drive a car and adjust the seat and steering wheel to your ideal position to see if both dimensions work for you. Are SUVs always the best option for tall people? Not necessarily. While many SUVs, like the Ford Bronco Sport and Subaru Forester, offer an upright seating position and generous headroom thanks to their boxy shape, some sedans and hatchbacks are surprisingly accommodating. The Genesis G80 and Kia K5, for example, provide ample front-seat legroom and well-designed cabins. The Subaru Impreza hatchback is also noted for having enough rear-seat space for six-footers. It's more about the specific model's design than its body style. Can I find a comfortable sports car if I'm tall? Yes, but it requires careful selection. Many sports cars are notoriously cramped, but some, like the BMW M2, offer a surprisingly spacious front row with good headroom and legroom once you're inside. The main trade-off is often ease of entry and exit, as sports cars sit low to the ground and may have heavily bolstered seats. If performance is a priority, it's worth testing a few options to see what works. What features should a tall person look for during a test drive? Look for a height-adjustable driver’s seat with a wide range of travel, a telescoping steering wheel (one that moves in and out, not just up and down), and good visibility from your natural seating position. Check for comfort features like power-adjustable seats with lumbar support, as seen in the Nissan Sentra, which can make a big difference on long drives. Also, perform the "me behind me" test: adjust the driver's seat for yourself, then sit in the back seat to see if there's enough room for passengers. What Makes CarGurus Best Cars Guides Different? Most car-shopping websites publish lists of the best cars across a variety of categories, with recommendations generally driven by editorial expertise. Here's what makes ours different: In addition to the insights and verdicts of our team of car-testing experts, our best cars guides take into account other factors that we know matter to buyers-real owner experiences and current market value. Our expert reviewers are among this country's most trusted automotive journalists, also writing for publications including US News and World Report, Edmunds, Digital Trends, J.D. Power, and Car & Driver. They put each car through real-world testing and create detailed reviews of performance in a range of categories, from practicality and driving manners to cost-effectiveness and safety. We also analyze hundreds of thousands of used car listings on CarGurus.com to track which models consistently offer the highest percentage of best deals relative to how many are listed for sale. Then we factor in reviews from owners-people who actually live with these cars every day. Our proprietary Best Cars algorithm then creates a final Overall CarGurus rating combining expert scores, user reviews, and the percentage of listings that have earned the Good or Great Deal rating. This multi-pronged approach reveals not just which cars excel on paper, but which ones deliver satisfaction and value when you're ready to buy.
